_meta: A metric that drifts over time on its own, measured under two experiment designs, used to show why a treatment must be compared against a CONCURRENT control -- both variants running at the same time on randomly split traffic -- rather than a before/after comparison across two time periods. Almost every real metric moves over time for reasons that have nothing to do with your change: seasonality, weekday-vs-weekend traffic, a marketing push, a slow shift in the user mix. A before/after design measures the old variant in one period and the new variant in a later period, so the difference it reports is the treatment effect PLUS whatever the metric drifted between the two periods -- the two are hopelessly confounded, and a time trend gets credited to (or blamed on) the treatment. A concurrent design runs both variants at the same time on a random split of the same traffic, so any time trend hits both arms equally and cancels out of their difference, leaving the treatment effect alone. base is the metric's baseline level in the first period; time_trend is how much the metric rises from the first period to the second for reasons unrelated to the treatment; true_effect is the real difference the new variant makes. These are the fixture; the metric value for each variant in each period, the before/after difference (old in period 1 vs new in period 2), and the concurrent difference (both in period 2) are computed.
